issues.legal_issue: An enactment passed by a body that was not the duly constituted legislature of the newly formed state is invalid.
material_facts: Two existing states ceased to exist and were united to form a new state with its own legislative assembly, prescribed to have 41 directly elected members.
A statute deemed the sitting members of the former assembly to have been elected to constituencies in the new state, while elections for the remaining seats were to be held separately.
Before the enactment was passed, no notification had formally constituted the new assembly, and the members had not taken a fresh oath or elected a Speaker for it.
The Governor’s notification called what it described as the second session of the assembly, although the new assembly had not previously held a session.
The body that passed the enactment proceeded as the former assembly; the enactment was challenged in petitions seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The body that passed the enactment was not the legislative assembly of the new state, so the enactment was not validly enacted. The court did not decide the separate challenge to the enactment’s substantive provisions.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 12 of the Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act, 1954, a new state and its legislative assembly were created. Section 15(1) of that Act deemed former assembly members elected to constituencies in the new state, but did not itself constitute the assembly; the further statutory steps for constituting it, including the notification contemplated by sections 73 and 74 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, remained necessary. Sections 14, 15(3), and 35 of the Government of Part C States Act, 1951, concerning oaths, proceedings despite vacancies, and protection against challenges for procedural irregularity, presupposed a duly constituted assembly and could not validate proceedings of a body that was not that assembly. Sections 14 and 16 of the New State Act did not alter that conclusion; nor did the possibility that a bill pending before the former assembly might lapse under section 25 of the Part C States Act. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_enactment and predecessor_states_replaced_by_new_state and former_members_deemed_elected and new_assembly_not_constituted and enactment_passed_by_called_body

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enactment: The proceeding challenged the validity of an enactment and sought constitutional relief against it.
predicates.predecessor_states_replaced_by_new_state: The former states ceased to exist and a new state with its own legislative assembly was formed from their territories.
predicates.former_members_deemed_elected: A statute deemed members of a former assembly elected to constituencies in the new state without a fresh election for those seats.
predicates.new_assembly_not_constituted: The required formal steps to bring the new assembly into being had not occurred, and the former members had not taken the required fresh oath or elected a Speaker for that assembly.
predicates.enactment_passed_by_called_body: The body convened as a session of the former assembly passed the challenged enactment.

issues.definition: When an enactment is challenged and passed by a body convened as the former assembly after a new state has replaced the predecessor states, deeming former members elected does not make that body the new assembly if the new assembly has not been constituted; the enactment is therefore invalid.
